claims.text: The initial material is monolithic, fully dense, as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g/cm³.
HfMoTaTiZr can be additively manufactured with an engineered lattice or porous core enclosed by a fully dense outer shell.
Directed energy deposition or electron-beam powder-bed fusion are suitable example processes for producing the proposed architecture.
The porous interior will reduce component mass and effective bulk density by removing material.
A dense, defect-minimized outer shell will bear the primary mechanical load.
The dense outer shell will preserve the necessary load path and dislocation-based strengthening mechanisms.
The proposed architecture will retain strength and ductility comparable to monolithic as-cast HfMoTaTiZr at room temperature.
The proposed architecture will retain strength and ductility comparable to monolithic as-cast HfMoTaTiZr near 1000 °C.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has established high mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures.
Mo contributes to higher room-temperature strength in equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr-derived alloys.
High-melting-point elements such as Mo, Nb, and Ta contribute to higher elevated-temperature strength in equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr-derived alloys.
Related NbTaHfTiZr-based refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit excellent room-temperature strength and ductility.
Mechanical-property retention will depend on lattice cell size, cell shape, porous volume fraction, and processing quality.
Defects or stress concentrations introduced by the lattice architecture could cause premature failure, particularly at elevated temperature.
The proposed architecture is intended for quasi-static and cyclic structural loading from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability includes cyclic loading, but the proposed experiment specifies only tensile and/or compression tests and does not test cyclic fatigue.

The prediction requires property retention at both room temperature and approximately 1000 °C, whereas the rejection rule requires excessive degradation at both temperatures; failure at only one required temperature would therefore not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
